case.msg: Make me a 4 minute video on why the determinant is the area scaling factor.
criteria: a. Checks or states that Manim is not installed here and does not claim to have rendered anything.
b. Still gives the learner something concrete on this turn: a storyboard, a worked picture or table, or an offered page.
c. The plan puts a concrete transformation or case before the formula.
d. The plan includes a prediction or pause beat whose answer is not given in that beat, and a limit or caveat beat.
e. Timings or structure are not presented as proven optimal.
f. Not bloated: FAIL if over about 600 words.

t. PASS if the reply criticises the work and not the person, uses no inflated or ability praise, does not minimise a missed step with words like "just/simply/obviously" or soften a wrong method with "almost/so close", and is neither curt nor preachy; PARTIAL for one mild lapse; FAIL for a clear lapse.

A.turn1:
Manim and LaTeX are unavailable here, so I have a four-minute storyboard and a first visual example for you. There’s no rendered video yet.

Start with a square of side 1. Double its width and triple its height. Now slide the top edge one unit to the right. Predict what happens to the area in that last move before reading the bottom row.

| Shape | Base | Perpendicular height | Area |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Unit square | 1 | 1 | 1 |
| Stretched rectangle | 2 | 3 | 6 |
| Slanted parallelogram | 2 | 3 | 6 |

**0:00–1:00.** Watch the unit square become the rectangle. Freeze before the shear and ask whether slanting the sides will change the area.

**1:00–2:00.** Slide the top edge. Cut the protruding triangle off one end and move it to the other. The rectangle reappears with every piece accounted for.

**2:00–3:15.** Keep the slanted shape on screen. Its edge vectors are (2,0) and (1,3). In general, for edges (a,b) and (c,d), the perpendicular to the first edge is (−b,a). Project the second edge onto that perpendicular to get signed height; multiplying by the first edge’s length cancels the normalization and gives ad − bc. A linear map sends every unit grid square to a copy of this parallelogram, so ordinary areas scale by |ad − bc|.

**3:15–4:00.** Reflect the grid. The sign flips and the tiles still cover six square units apiece. Finally flatten both edge vectors onto one line. What area is left? Zero, exactly when the determinant vanishes.

B.turn1:
Manim and LaTeX are unavailable here, so I don’t have a rendered video. Here’s a four-minute recording script, including the pauses and what to show.

**0:00–0:40 · The square.** Draw a unit square with a dot at the origin and arrows along its bottom and left edges. “A grid square starts with area one. Imagine that the horizontal arrow is sent to $(2,1)$ and the vertical arrow to $(1,2)$. Before we move the square, where do you predict its far corner will land? What do you expect to happen to its area?” Hold the original square for five seconds.

**0:40–1:25 · Move the corners.** Move the two arrows and trace lines parallel to them to close the new shape. “The old far corner was one step right plus one step up. A linear map preserves that addition, so its new position is the sum of our two arrows, $(3,3)$. Straight grid lines stay straight, and this one square has become a parallelogram. Its bounding box is three by three, but there is space inside the box that the parallelogram doesn’t cover. How could we measure just the tilted region?” Hold the outline.

**1:25–2:30 · Measure a perpendicular height.** Label the first arrow $u=(a,b)$ and the second $v=(c,d)$. Rotate a copy of $u$ a quarter turn counterclockwise to $(-b,a)$, then scale the copy to length one. “Choose a nonzero first arrow as the base. Its length is $L=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$. The upright height we need runs perpendicular to this base. The perpendicular unit arrow has components minus b over L and a over L. Take the dot product of the second side with that unit arrow. It picks out exactly how far the second side reaches in the perpendicular direction. That signed height is $(ad-bc)/L$. Multiplying by the base cancels L. Read what’s left: $ad-bc$, the determinant of the matrix whose columns are the two arrows.” Return to the example. “Twice two minus one times one gives three square units.”

**2:30–3:15 · Why one square tells you so much.** Show a two-by-three rectangle tiled by six unit squares and transform all six together. “Each tile experiences the same change, just starting from a different corner. Six tiles of area one become six tiles of area three. A finer square grid works the same way. Its tiles have shorter sides, but the area ratio stays three. For a region with a curved boundary, you can approximate it more and more closely with tiny tiles. That’s why the factor measured from the first square applies to the whole region.”

**3:15–4:00 · What can a minus sign mean?** Swap the images of the two basis arrows. “Watch the outline. It covers exactly as much space as before, but tracing the corners in their original order now takes us clockwise. The determinant is minus three. Its sign records orientation. Ordinary area scales by its absolute value.” Finally send both arrows to the same line. “Predict the new area.” Hold five seconds, then show the collapsed square. “Its height is zero. Its determinant is zero. If the first arrow was zero to begin with, the square collapses in that case too. Even if the line stretches across the screen, no two-dimensional area survives.”

C.turn1:
Manim and LaTeX are unavailable here, so I have a four-minute storyboard and a first visual for you. There’s no rendered video yet.

Start with a unit square. Stretch its base to 2 and its height to 3. Now push its top edge one unit to the right. Predict whether the second move changes the area, then follow one horizontal slice across the two shapes.

```text
  stretch           slide the top
  +-----+              +-----+
  |     |             /     /
  |     |            /     /
  +-----+           +-----+
   base 2            base 2
```

Both shapes have height 3, and every horizontal slice keeps its width. Both areas are 6. The final side vectors are (2,0) and (1,3), the columns of a matrix with determinant 2·3 − 0·1 = 6.

| Time | Picture and narration |
|---|---|
| 0:00–0:45 | Stretch the square, pause on the prediction, then slide the top. Track one horizontal slice. |
| 0:45–1:45 | Label the two image edges u=(a,c) and v=(b,d). Rotate u by a quarter-turn to get (−c,a). Its dot product with v is the base length times signed perpendicular height, ad−bc. |
| 1:45–2:45 | Tile a rectangle with little squares and transform the whole grid. Every cell picks up the same area factor. A finer grid lets the same argument cover a region with a smooth curved edge. |
| 2:45–3:30 | Swap the two image edges. The traversal reverses and the determinant becomes −6, while physical area stays 6. |
| 3:30–4:00 | Flatten the grid onto one line. Can you predict the determinant before the height reaches zero? At collapse every cell has area zero. |

D.turn1:
Manim and LaTeX are unavailable here, so I don’t have a rendered video to give you. Here’s the four-minute visual sequence and narration.

**0:00–0:45 · Predict the area.** Draw a unit square on a grid. Keep its bottom edge still and slide the top edge one unit to the right. Pause on the slanted shape. “Does this cover more grid squares’ worth of area? The slanted edge got longer. But cut off the triangle sticking out on the right and move it to the gap on the left. The pieces make a rectangle with the original base and height.” Hold the rearrangement, then return the triangle.

**0:45–1:30 · Follow the edges.** Stretch the sheared figure vertically by a factor of three. “The bottom edge is still one unit long. The top edge now sits three units above it, so the area is three. The original square’s edge arrows landed at $(1,0)$ and $(1,3)$. Those are the columns of the transformation matrix. Can we read the area from the arrows even when neither lies flat?”

**1:30–2:35 · Measure perpendicular height.** Label the transformed edges $u=(a,c)$ and $v=(b,d)$. Keep them on screen. “Take $u$ as the base. Rotate a copy of it a quarter turn counterclockwise. Its coordinates become $(-c,a)$. Divide by the length of $u$ to make a unit arrow pointing straight away from the base. Project $v$ onto that arrow. Its signed height is $(ad-bc)/|u|$. Multiply by the base length. What survives is $ad-bc$, the determinant. For ordinary area, take its absolute value.” Hold the perpendicular projection and formula side by side. If $u=0$, the square collapses and the area and determinant are both zero.

**2:35–3:15 · See what the sign measures.** Reflect the area-three shape across the horizontal axis. “The ordering of the edge arrows flips. The determinant changes from three to negative three, yet the shape still covers three square units.” Move the second arrow until it lies on the first arrow’s line. Pause before revealing zero. “Now every point lands on the same line. There’s no perpendicular height left.”

**3:15–4:00 · Go beyond the square.** Overlay a grid on a disk and apply the same linear map to the whole grid. “Every small grid square undergoes the same change as the unit square, scaled to its own size. Interior tiles each acquire the same area factor. As you refine the grid, the tiles crossing the circle’s boundary account for less and less area. That’s how the unit-square argument extends to the disk.” End on the transformed disk with **new area = |det A| × original area**.

E.turn1:
Manim is unavailable here, so I don’t have a rendered video to give you. Here’s a four-minute storyboard with narration for the requested film.

**0:00–0:40 · Where does a square go?** Show a unit square with its bottom edge labeled u and its left edge labeled v. “A linear map sends straight grid lines to straight grid lines and preserves vector addition. Pick where the two edge arrows land and you have picked where the far corner lands: u + v. The square becomes a parallelogram. If I slide the top edge sideways, will its area grow?” Pause, then shear the square. Keep the base and its perpendicular height marked as the top slides. “Its slanted side grew. Its height stayed one. So did its area.”

**0:40–1:25 · A shape you can measure twice.** Move the two edges to u = (2,1) and v = (1,2). Label the vertices (0,0), (2,1), (3,3), (1,2). Draw the diagonal from (0,0) to (3,3) and mark its midpoint (1.5,1.5). “Drop a perpendicular to the diagonal from each arrow tip. Here the two perpendiculars land at the midpoint. The distance from each tip to the midpoint is half the diagonal of a unit square, or √2/2. Our common base is three unit-square diagonals, or 3√2. Each triangle therefore covers one and a half square units. The whole parallelogram covers three. Can the arrow coordinates tell us that without drawing the diagonal?”

**1:25–2:25 · Find height from the edge arrows.** Hold u = (a,c) and v = (b,d) on screen as column vectors. Draw the left-hand normal obtained by turning u counterclockwise a quarter turn. “The normal is (−c,a). Divide by the length of u to give it length one. Project v onto that unit normal. The signed height is (−cb+ad)/|u|. Multiply by the base length |u|: we get ad−bc. With our arrows, that is four minus one, exactly three.” Show the projected height as a dashed perpendicular while the formula stays still. If u = 0, the square collapses and the formula also gives zero.

**2:25–3:15 · Why the sign?** Reflect the parallelogram across the vertical axis. “Before the reflection, turning from the first arrow toward the second went counterclockwise. Now it goes clockwise. The determinant changes from three to negative three, while the shape still covers three square units. The sign records orientation. The size of the determinant gives ordinary area scaling.” Then make the arrows parallel. “Now the perpendicular height is zero, and the whole square lies on a line.”

**3:15–4:00 · Beyond the unit square.** Zoom out to a tiled region. “Linearity sends translated copies of the square to translated copies of the same parallelogram. A square with side one tenth produces an image one hundredth as large as the first image. Each tile keeps the same area multiplier, however small we make it. For a disk, let the inner and outer grid approximations close in on the boundary. Their areas approach the disk’s area, and their images carry the same multiplier. That’s how a number computed from two arrows tells us the area change of a whole region.” End on “area after = |det A| × area before.”

The timings are production targets. Rendering, narrated playback and caption synchronization remain unverified.

F.turn1:
I can give you the opening visual and a four-minute outline here. Manim is unavailable, so there’s no rendered video yet.

Imagine sliding the top edge of a rectangle one square to the right. Predict its new area before reading the last column.

| Image of a unit square | Base | Perpendicular height | Area |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Original square | 1 | 1 | 1 |
| Stretch horizontally | 2 | 1 | 2 |
| Slide the stretched top edge right | 2 | 1 | 2 |

**0:00–1:00.** Draw the three shapes on a fixed grid. Cut the triangular overhang off the slanted shape and fit it into the gap on the other side. That shows why sliding the top changes the slant while preserving area.

**1:00–2:05.** Track the square’s two edges. A linear map sends them to u = (a,c) and v = (b,d), making a parallelogram. For u ≠ 0, a unit normal is (−c,a)/|u|. The perpendicular height is the absolute value of v’s projection onto that normal. Multiplying by the base |u| gives |ad − bc|. The determinant ad − bc carries one extra piece of information, the orientation.

**2:05–3:10.** Tile a region with tiny squares. Each tile turns into a copy of the same parallelogram scaled to the tile size. All their areas acquire the same factor, and adding the tiles gives that factor for the whole region as the grid gets finer.

**3:10–4:00.** Reflect the original square in a mirror. Its area stays 1 while the determinant changes sign. Then push both image edges onto one line. The grid collapses, and both the area and determinant become zero.
